clue.text: Annual occurrence, that's splendid, of a race,

parts.note: splendid means grand, magnificent
of a race means national, belonging to a people or nation

explanation.surface: Someone praises a yearly sporting event as a splendid race.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is a famous steeplechase run every year at Aintree, near Liverpool. 'of a race' is not the horse race but a people: national.
explanation.definitionFit: The steeplechase is held once every year, so it is a yearly event.

clue.text: Titanic crossing from Antrim by this?

definitions.text: Titanic crossing from Antrim by this?

parts.words: Titanic crossing from Antrim by this?
parts.note: legend says a giant built a stone road across the sea from County Antrim to Scotland, so a titanic crossing

explanation.surface: It asks whether the doomed liner set sail from Northern Ireland this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' suggests the liner built in Belfast, but it means gigantic; the giant Finn McCool supposedly built the road.
explanation.definitionFit: The basalt columns on the County Antrim coast are named as a giant's path toward Scotland.

clue.text: Change so to speak one's name before it

definitions.text: Change so to speak one's name before it

indicators.note: so to speak signals we take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: to change is to alter

explanation.surface: A rule that changing one's name requires standing before a certain place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a bride traditionally takes a new surname at the church altar.
explanation.definitionFit: At a wedding the couple stand before the communion table, where a bride often takes a new surname.

clue.text: Medics, at heart, not believing symptom

indicators.note: at heart means take the central letters of the word medics

parts.note: an agnostic does not believe in God, holding it unknowable

explanation.surface: Doctors, deep down, don't trust some sign of illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagnostic is a distinguishing sign that helps identify a disease, much like a symptom.

clue.text: Sea ship wrecked — in a word, a loss

indicators.note: wrecked suggests a ship broken up, so the letters of sea and ship are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shipwreck at sea is, in short, a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a word' looks like 'briefly', but is literal: the loss happens within a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphesis is the dropping of an unstressed vowel at the start of a word, as in 'squire' from 'esquire'.

clue.text: Being cut makes us go red in embarrassment

indicators.note: embarrassment suggests confusion and disorder, so the letters of go red in are rearranged

explanation.surface: A social snub makes us blush with embarrassment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' belongs to the letters being rearranged, so 'embarrassment' alone signals it.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut someone is to snub them, deliberately passing them by unnoticed.

clue.text: A VIP with his writers

definitions.meaning: a jokey title for a self-important person
pen points, the parts of pens that write

explanation.definitionFit: His Nibs mocks a grandee; nibs are the metal tips of fountain pens that do the writing.

clue.text: Muck, being filthy, is proverbially so

definitions.text: Muck, being filthy, is proverbially so

parts.words: Muck, being filthy, is proverbially so
parts.note: money is proverbially muck and 'filthy lucre', and the saying goes 'where there's muck there's brass', so dirty work pays

explanation.surface: Dirt is famously profitable, as the saying goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muck' and 'filthy' point to dirt, but both are slang for money: 'filthy lucre', and the northern English saying 'where there's muck there's brass' (money).
explanation.definitionFit: Something profitable brings in plenty of money, and money is the proverbial filthy lucre.

clue.text: Cockney's fruitful means of getting a rise

definitions.text: Cockney's fruitful means of getting a rise

parts.words: Cockney's fruitful means of getting a rise
parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang a pair of fruits stands for the stairs, which take you up

explanation.surface: A Londoner's productive way of winning a pay increase.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang, from London's East End, swaps a word for a phrase that rhymes with it; here fruit for stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming slang names two fruits for a flight of stairs, the way one climbs up.

clue.text: Aim of RAF official in 22, to collar material

parts.note: the RAF motto is Per ardua ad astra, 'through adversity to the stars', so its aim is the stars, Latin astra
22 across is ASIA, and a khan is a ruler or official in Central Asia

explanation.surface: An RAF officer serving in the East aims to grab some cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: Answers to other clues are referred to by number: 22 is the across answer meaning Asia. The Royal Air Force's Latin motto ends 'ad astra'.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrakhan is a curly lambskin fur often used to trim coat collars.

clue.text: Taxi turns up in Lancashire

indicators.note: turns tells us the word for a taxi is read from right to left

parts.note: a taxi is a cab
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cab doing a U-turn and arriving in a northern English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacup is a small mill town found in the county of Lancashire, in north-west England.

clue.text: Italian city — one captured in the revolution

indicators.note: captured in means held inside, so the letter for one goes within the word for a revolution

parts.note: a revolution is one turn of a wheel
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A revolutionary in an Italian city is taken prisoner during the uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolution' suggests political upheaval, but here it is a single rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin is the capital of Piedmont in north-west Italy.

clue.text: Jack takes it to be ridiculous, irrational

indicators.note: Jack plus 'it' makes the word for ridiculous, so 'it' is that word with the sailor's letters taken off

parts.note: ridiculous means absurd
a jack is a sailor, abbreviated AB for able seaman

explanation.surface: A man named Jack considers some notion absurd and irrational.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (AB) taking 'it' gives ABSURD, so 'it' is ABSURD with AB removed.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a surd is a root that is an irrational number, such as the square root of two.

clue.text: Many are not well fitted for the post

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: Lots of people are too sick to be appointed to the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fitted for' reads as part of the surface but links the wordplay to the definition; 'post' is letters, not a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail and post are synonyms for letters and parcels sent through the postal service.

clue.text: Disagreeable as a .. French money-grabbing rustic

parts.note: un is the French for a

indicators.note: grabbing means holding on to, so the countryman's word takes in the money letter

parts.note: a rustic is a country person, a peasant
L is the sign for the pound, money

explanation.surface: A greedy French countryman is described as nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'money-grabbing' looks like 'greedy', but splits: L (pound sterling) is grabbed by PEASANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unpleasant is disagreeable, nasty or not enjoyable.

clue.text: Some such assistance as basis for body-building

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A little help like this is the foundation for building up muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body-building' suggests a gym, but the body here is a car body built on a frame.
explanation.definitionFit: A chassis is the base frame of a vehicle on which its bodywork is mounted.

clue.text: Fall on 26, say, with a firearm

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is pronounced and the sound gives the letters

parts.note: Fall is the American autumn, and 26 across is ATTIC, joined on after it

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles onto a top-floor answer while carrying a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Answers to other clues are referred to by number: 26 is the across answer meaning a loft. 'Fall' is not a tumble but the season.
explanation.definitionFit: An automatic is a self-loading pistol or rifle that keeps firing.

clue.text: Smart guys, reporting Defoe's conclusion

parts.note: the novelist Defoe's first name was Daniel, shortened to Dan
a conclusion is how a story ends, and Defoe's life ended when he died: Dan dies

explanation.surface: Well-dressed men give an account of how a novel by Defoe ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Daniel Defoe wrote Robinson Crusoe; his 'conclusion' is his death, which a reporter would headline 'Dan dies'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dandies are men devoted to fashionable dress, like fops.

clue.text: Only accused of being not experienced

definitions.meaning: someone merely accused has not yet faced trial in court
lacking experience, never tested in practice

explanation.definitionFit: An accused person awaiting trial has not been put on trial yet, and a novice has never been put to the test.

clue.text: Row about broken bust — now fit only for this

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for a row goes around the rest

parts.note: a din is a noisy row

indicators.note: broken means smashed, so the letters of bust are rearranged

explanation.surface: An argument ends with a smashed statue that can only be thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts USTB (the anagram of BUST, from 'broken') inside DIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish fit only to be thrown out goes into a refuse bin.

clue.text: Irish lass gives officer the general direction

parts.note: COL is short for colonel, an army officer
Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general in the American Civil War
N is north, a compass direction

explanation.surface: An Irish girl tells an officer roughly which way to go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'general direction' reads as one phrase meaning roughly where, but splits into a general and a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Colleen comes from the Irish word for a girl and is used for an Irish young woman.

clue.text: Stop the war-trumpet

definitions.meaning: an organ stop, a set of pipes the organist switches on
a shrill trumpet once used to rally troops in battle

explanation.definitionFit: A clarion is both an organ register with a trumpet tone and a medieval battle bugle.

clue.text: She put an end to a doctor's difficulty

indicators.note: put an end to means keep only the tail end of the word, losing its opening letters

parts.note: The Doctor's Dilemma is a play by George Bernard Shaw, so a doctor's difficulty is a dilemma

explanation.surface: A woman resolved the problem facing a physician.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's play The Doctor's Dilemma supplies the word; only its closing four letters are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is a woman's name, so it can stand for 'she', a female person.

clue.text: "Eastern 'parts" as one article has it

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper article describes eastern regions in a certain way.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia is the continent of the East, covering the Orient's lands.

clue.text: Fabulous slave's main turn work

indicators.note: turn tells us the word for the main is read backwards

parts.note: the main is a poetic word for the open sea
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A legendary slave's chief task is to turn round and get to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like chief but is the old word for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was reputedly a slave in ancient Greece, and is known as the teller of fables.

clue.text: For Moses the height of vice — sloth

parts.note: a vice is a sin
the ai is the three-toed sloth of South America

explanation.surface: For Moses, idleness is the ultimate wickedness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sloth' suggests the deadly sin, but is the animal; 'vice' gives the sin.
explanation.definitionFit: Moses climbed the mountain in the Sinai desert to receive the Ten Commandments.

clue.text: The Tale of Peter Rabbit sound definition

definitions.text: The Tale of Peter Rabbit sound definition

parts.words: The Tale of Peter Rabbit sound definition
parts.note: the book title's 'Tale' heard aloud is 'tail', so this defines the tail of Peter Rabbit

explanation.surface: A precise description of a famous children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Beatrix Potter's book title reads as a story, but said aloud 'Tale' becomes the short tail of a rabbit.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

clue.text: This salt for one enjoying high living?

definitions.meaning: ... salt is the refined wit associated with ancient Athens
a room right at the top of a house is where someone lives high up

explanation.definitionFit: Attic salt means elegant Athenian wit; a garret under the roof is a lofty place to live.

clue.text: Waives the rule, does she, speaking out of order?

definitions.text: Waives the rule, does she, speaking out of order?

parts.words: Waives the rule, does she, speaking out of order?
parts.note: the patriotic song says this figure rules the waves; muddle the words when speaking and she waives the rule

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a woman is breaking the rules by talking out of turn.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'Rule, Britannia!' has the line 'rule the waves'; the clue garbles it into 'waives the rule'.
explanation.definitionFit: The female figure personifying Britain is the one said in the song to rule the waves.

clue.text: One ending for every life with this scourge?

definitions.text: One ending for every life with this scourge?

parts.words: One ending for every life with this scourge?
parts.note: a cat has nine lives, and this whip has one tail, or ending, for each of them

explanation.surface: A grim remark that a plague brings each life to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' suggests death, but it is the tail of a lash; cats proverbially have nine lives.
explanation.definitionFit: This whip of nine knotted cords was a scourge used for flogging sailors and prisoners.
